title: Access Boundaries: Terraform scaffold for least-privilege roles & policies
creator: Ava Martinez
description: Deliver a reusable Terraform module that bootstraps an access-boundary layer for Private (VPC) deployments. The module will create opinionated, environment-scoped role constructs, permission boundaries, and policy templates to enforce least-privilege for Redwood platform components (control plane agents, node bootstrap, logging/metrics shipper, upgrade operator). Goals: 1) provide a single source-of-truth for baseline roles so downstream customers and the Private install playbook can be minimal and auditable; 2) enable safe upgrades (schema changes in policies) with a migration plan and roll-forward/rollback hooks; 3) include integrated health checks and drift detection patterns to detect permission regressions after upgrades.
acceptance_criteria: Module published to internal Terraform registry with semantic versioning (v0.1.0) and a clear CHANGELOG entry
Module API documented (variables/outputs) in Confluence with example usage for a 3-account VPC install (control, shared-services, workload)
Automated plan/apply CI job that runs a dry-run in a sandbox org and validates policies against a minimal test harness (see test_plan)
Migration guide covering two upgrade scenarios: (A) additive permissions; (B) permission narrowing that requires staged rollout and operator restart
Security review completed and sign-off by Security team; any high-risk findings mitigated or accepted
Health check Lambda (or equivalent) example included that verifies critical API calls succeed using the provisioned roles
No customer-facing outages expected from the initial rollout; mitigation playbook included in docs
implementation_notes: Design decisions: 1) Provide three canonical role archetypes: bootstrap_actor (least privileges to bootstrap nodes), control_plane_agent (narrowed to required API ops), and observability_shipper (write-only to monitoring sinks). 2) Use permission boundaries to limit any role's expansion by downstream modules; enforce via 'aws_iam_policy' and 'aws_iam_role_policy_attachment' patterns. 3) Avoid inline policies for long-term maintenance—emit managed policies with predictable names to ease upgrades. 4) Ensure variables allow account-scoped ARNs and an optional 'extra_permissions' map for customer overrides, but require approval flag to enable non-standard additions. 5) To support upgrades, module will export an 'upgrade_plan' output (string URL to generated plan artifact) and emit a tagging convention (iam:module-version) for drift detection. Trade-offs: keeping policies managed increases AWS-managed-policy count but enables clean versioning; using permission boundaries adds an extra layer of complexity but gives safer upgrades. Implementation steps: prototype policies in policies/ directory, write Terraform module under modules/access-boundary, create examples/ for single-account and three-account installs, wire up CI that runs terratest/runner to validate permissions.
test_plan: 1) Unit: policy linting using cloud-custodian and tfsec in CI. 2) Integration: sandbox deploy of module in a disposable AWS org account using GH Actions (plan-only, then apply to a temporary infra using ephemeral creds). 3) Behavioral: run a small test harness (python script) that assumes role via sts:AssumeRole and performs representative API calls (describe-instances, s3:PutObject to logging bucket, kms:Encrypt for KMS write operations) to assert nothing is over/under-provisioned. 4) Upgrade tests: simulate v0.1.0 -> v0.2.0 where v0.2.0 narrows one permission; validate staged rollout pattern where control-plane rollouts use canary nodes and rollback occurs automatically if health-check fails.

rollback_plan: If an upgrade narrows permissions and a health check fails, the CI/CD pipeline will: 1) stop rollout and open a rollback job; 2) reapply previous module version by pinning module source to the prior tag; 3) run post-rollback health checks; 4) notify on-call (pager) and document incident in postmortem. Playbook includes required steps for manual IAM fix via console if automation fails.
operational_checks:
- Drift detection: nightly job queries tagged policies/roles and compares current inline/attached policy versions with registry.
- Health checks: example Lambda that attempts key control-plane operations using each canonical role and pushes metrics to the priv-iam Grafana dashboard.
- Alerting: critical alerts if any health-check returns 5xx or AccessDenied; auto-create ticket in Jira with attached logs and replay commands.
